title: The ark (Genesis 6:14–7:24)
hookLine: a box of wood, pairs of every creature, forty days of rain
tomorrow: the dove and the olive leaf

cards: God's instructions to Noah read like a lumber order. Gopher wood. Rooms inside.
Pitch, inside and out. Three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, thirty high. Three decks, a window, a door in the side.
Then the passengers: a male and a female of every living kind, and of the clean animals, seven and seven, the text says. Food for all of them.
Then the fountains of the deep break open, the windows of heaven open, and it rains forty days and forty nights. The water rises above the mountains and stays a hundred and fifty days.

teach.h: TEVAH — A BOX, NOT A SHIP.
teach.b: The Hebrew for the ark is tevah, and it doesn't mean a ship. Look at what's missing: no sail, no rudder, no oars, no one steering. A tevah is a box, a chest.
It doesn't go anywhere. It floats, and keeps what's inside alive. The word turns up again, in Exodus.
A mother hides her baby from Pharaoh's soldiers in a little basket daubed with pitch, and sets it in the reeds by the Nile.

teach.h: MOSES' BASKET IS A TEVAH TOO.
teach.b: That basket is a tevah. The baby is Moses. Two boxes, one enormous and one tiny, both covered with pitch, both steered by no one, both carrying the future of the world on dark water.
Why did the building take so long?
One midrash says Noah spent a hundred and twenty years on it, planting the trees and cutting them, so that people would ask what he was doing, and have a chance to change. Nobody did.
A teaching in the Talmud says his year in the ark was mostly one job: feeding every creature at its own hour, day and night. The hero of the flood spent it hauling food to animals.
Later, a Hasidic reading played on tevah also meaning a word: step into the words of your prayer the way Noah stepped into the ark. But the plain story is simpler.
When the world is drowning, the task is to carry what's alive.

how: Jews read the flood story in the autumn as part of the weekly Torah portion Noach; Jewish law also counts care for animals, such as feeding them before oneself, as a duty.

o: a box with no sail, made to keep life afloat
the gold chest that held the tablets of the law
a great ship Noah steered to a new land

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah says every animal came aboard in just one pair
a male and female of every kind, and of the clean animals, seven and seven.
the ark had no sail and no rudder
a tevah is a box. it floats, and nobody steers it.
the whole flood was over in forty days
the rain fell forty days; the water stayed high a hundred and fifty, and Noah's family was aboard about a year.

games.q: you're Noah, and God has told you to build a huge box for every living thing. the neighbors watch you cut trees. what do you do?
o: build fast and keep it secret.
build slowly, in the open, so people ask why.
games.why: one midrash says Noah took a hundred and twenty years, so people would ask and have time to change. nobody did.

practice: Bring to mind one living thing that depends on you: a pet, a plant on the windowsill, a child, a parent, a friend in a hard stretch.
Picture it clearly, and ask what it needs from you this week: water, a walk, food at the right hour. Nothing heroic; Noah's work was mostly feeding.

wordCard.voice: The ark. In Hebrew, tevah: a box with no sail and no rudder, built to keep life afloat.

orig.note: Hebrew: a box or chest. used in the Torah for Noah's ark and for the basket of baby Moses.

carryVoice: Your line: carry what's alive. Tomorrow, a dove, and what she brings back. Day thirty-three, done.
